class.name: GDScriptTrait
class.brief_description: A reusable bundle of members that classes can include with the [code]uses[/code] keyword.
class.description:
A trait is declared with the [code]trait[/code] keyword and holds any member a class can hold, except inner classes. Classes bring a trait's members into themselves with [code]uses[/code]. [codeblock] trait Damageable: const MAX_HEALTH := 100 var health: int = MAX_HEALTH
func take_damage(amount: int) -> void: health -= amount
func is_dead() -> bool: return health <= 0
class Player extends Node: uses Damageable
# The class's own version takes precedence over the trait's. func take_damage(amount: int) -> void: health -= amount * 2 [/codeblock] [b]Copying, not inheriting:[/b] When a class uses a trait, the trait's members are copied into that class. This is what separates a trait from a base class: every class that uses the trait gets its own copy of its variables, so two classes using the same trait do not share state. A trait is not in the inheritance chain, so it has no parent and no children of its own. [b]A trait that describes a whole file:[/b] Writing [code]trait Name[/code] on its own, without a body, declares that the script file itself is the trait, in the style of [code]class_name[/code]. The file's top level members (its variables, constants, functions and signals) then belong to that trait, which keeps one trait per file: [codeblock] # damageable.gd trait Damageable
var health: int = 100
func take_damage(amount: int) -> void: health -= amount [/codeblock] Such a trait is registered globally, so any script can use it by name. Only one trait can describe a file, and it must be written at the top level of that file. [b]Traits are not base types:[/b] A trait is not a type, so it cannot be instantiated, and using it in [code]extends[/code], as a type hint, in an [code]as[/code] cast or in a typed container is an error. To use a trait, declare it and then [code]uses[/code] it from a class. A class can use several traits by writing one [code]uses[/code] statement per trait. [b]Overriding members:[/b] A member declared on the class itself always wins over a trait member with the same name. Declaring a function with a trait's signature in the class overrides the trait's implementation, which is how a trait can offer a default that a class customizes. [b]Errors:[/b] A trait cannot contain inner classes or other traits. Using the same trait more than once in one class is an error. Calling a trait's functions directly, through a trait reference rather than an instance, is an error, because a trait has no instance of its own — call them on a class that uses it. [b]Traits across files:[/b] A trait declared at the top level of a script is known to the whole project, so another script can use it by name with [code]uses[/code]. A trait declared inside an inner class is only reachable from that file, written with dots as [code]uses Inner.SomeTrait[/code]. [b]Type tests:[/b] [code]value is SomeTrait[/code] answers whether the class of [code]value[/code] took that trait, directly or through a base class. Like [code]is SomeClass[/code], it asks about the value itself: when the class of [code]value[/code] is known to take the trait, the answer is decided while the script is analyzed and costs nothing at runtime; otherwise the value's script is asked at runtime, so a value whose static type is a base class or [Variant] still gets the correct answer.
